title: Feds seek more than $100 million in lawsuit against owners of Dali
summary: The Justice Department said Wednesday it is suing the owners of the cargo ship that caused the collapse of the Francis Scott Key Bridge, seeking $100 million for the cost of cleaning up the debris and unspecified punitive damages.
content:
by Bryan P. Sears, Maryland Matters September 18, 2024

by Bryan P. Sears, Maryland Matters September 18, 2024

The Justice Department said Wednesday it is suing the owners of the cargo ship that caused the collapse of the Francis Scott Key Bridge, seeking unspecified punitive damages and $100 million for the cost of cleaning up the debris.

The civil lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court in Baltimore, said the owners and operators of the container ship Dali “sent an ill-prepared crew on an abjectly unseaworthy vessel to navigate the United States’ waterways …  Yet they cut corners in ways that risked lives and infrastructure. Those responsible for the vessel must be held fully accountable for the catastrophic harm they caused.”

The suit goes on to say that punitive damages “should be imposed to deter such misconduct” in the future. The lawsuit names Grace Ocean Private Limited and Synergy Marine Private Limited, the Singaporean corporations that own and operate the Dali, respectively.

“This accident happened because of the careless and grossly negligent decisions made by Grace Ocean and Synergy, who recklessly chose to send an unseaworthy vessel to navigate a critical waterway and ignore the risks to American lives and the nation’s infrastructure,” Acting Deputy Assistant Attorney General Chetan Patil said in conference call announcing the suit.

Darrell Wilson, a spokesperson for Grace Ocean and Synergy, said the lawsuit “was anticipated” because of a September deadline set by the court.

“The owner and manager will have no further comment on the merits of any claim at this time, but we do look forward to our day in court to set the record straight,” Wilson said in a statement.

Widow of welder killed in Key Bridge collapse calls for safer working conditions

The crash occurred in the early morning hours of March 26 when the fully loaded Dali lost power on its way out of the Port of Baltimore. With no steering, the 985-foot ship, weighing 95,000 gross tons, slammed into a bridge tower, causing the center span of the bridge to tumble into the Patapsco River.

The allision killed six workers who were on the bridge, shut down traffic to and from the Port of Baltimore for months and destroyed the span over the Patapsco.

The lawsuit said the power outage was caused by excessive vibrations that caused power cables to come loose on the ship. It said the owners and operators of the ship knew of the vibration problems, but jury-rigged low-cost solutions that failed when needed, and that a series of other shortcuts led to a “cascading series of failures” that resulted in the crash.

“In so many ways, the Key Bridge has symbolized the resilience of our state and our nation in a very real way,” said Erek Barron, U.S. attorney for the District of Maryland. “For many people, the Key Bridge was a pathway to the American dream. A part of our national culture is now gone. Those responsible for the Key Bridge collapse must be held accountable.”

The suit filed Wednesday is separate from pending legal action by the state, which hopes to recover damages that could help pay for the replacement of the bridge. That project is estimated to cost $1.7 billion.

Principal Deputy Associate Attorney General Benjamin Mizer said  the catastrophe in March was avoidable, laying blame on the owners of the ship, whom he said operated a vessel with known problems.

“We allege that the Dali’s owner and operator recklessly cut corners in ways that risk lives and the economic well-being of the nation,” Mizer said. “As a result, when the Dali lost power, a cascading set of failures led to disaster.

“The United States spent more than $100 million responding to this disaster, to clear the channel and to reopen the Port of Baltimore. Those costs should be borne by the ship’s owner and operator, not the American taxpayer,” he said.

Toll authority approves initial Key Bridge replacement contract

Even though the lawsuit cited ship vibrations in the power outage, the final cause of the Dali’s power failure, and the bridge collapse, remain the subject of an ongoing investigation by the National Transportation Safety Board.

As part of its findings, the Justice Department alleges that the ship’s electrical system “long suffered the effects of heavy vibrations, a well-known cause of transformer and electrical failure.” Federal attorneys allege the owner and operator jury-rigged the ship with retro-fitted antivibration devices that cracked over time, were welded back together, and cracked again.

“And they also wedged a metal cargo hook between the transformer and a nearby steel beam, in a makeshift attempt to limit vibration,” according to the lawsuit.

The government further claims that the ship used substandard pumps that prevented adequate flow of fuel to emergency generators. The lack of proper fuel pressure caused the second blackout.

And when the pilot ordered the crew to drop anchor, in an effort to keep the ship from striking the bridge, the anchor “was not ready for immediate release,” the suit said. A “last-ditch attempt” to use a thruster failed because the bow thruster was “unavailable,” according to the lawsuit.

“These configurations caused the ship to lose power, which led to subsequent equipment failures, culminating in the Dali striking one of the piers of the Francis Scott Key Bridge and causing the bridge to collapse into the Fort McHenry channel,” Patil said.

Mizer said the findings outlined in the lawsuit filed Wednesday stem from a separate, parallel Justice Department review. The incident is also the subject of an ongoing criminal investigation.

YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE.

Mizer said it is rare for the federal government to  seek punitive damages, as it is in this case.

“But we do so when it is warranted by egregious facts like those in this case,” Mizer said. “And the reason we do that is to not only hold accountable those who we allege are responsible, but also to deter not only the vessel, owner and operator, but also others from engaging in such reckless behavior.”
